prog-ma-001.question: A patient has a Medtronic dual-chamber pacemaker programmed to MVP mode, with slow sinus rhythm at rest. Based on the tracing, in which mode is the device operating at this moment?
options: AAI(R) with ventricular channel monitoring
DDI(R) after mode switching for atrial arrhythmia
Backup VVI(R) running below the lower rate
DDD(R) with an AV delay extended by hysteresis search
commentaires: Correct: an atrial spike followed by a narrow conducted QRS, with no ventricular spike: MVP is operating in AAI(R) while monitoring the ventricle.
Incorrect: DDI(R) is the fallback mode for mode switching on atrial arrhythmia; here the atrium is paced and conducts normally.
Incorrect: backup VVI at a reduced rate is the logic of RYTHMIQ (Boston Scientific); it is not the MVP fallback.
Incorrect: staying in DDD while extending the AV delay is the principle of AV hysteresis (Abbott VIP, Boston Scientific AV Search+), not of MVP.
prog-ma-001.explication: The tracing shows an atrial spike followed by a P wave and then a narrow conducted QRS, with no ventricular spike. MVP is an atrial-based mode: as long as AV conduction is present, the device operates in AAI(R) while monitoring the ventricular channel (often referred to as AAI/R+). It only switches to DDD(R) when loss of AV conduction is confirmed. Staying in DDD with an extended AV delay is the logic of AV hysteresis (VIP in Abbott devices, AV Search+ in Boston Scientific devices). Backup VVI at a reduced rate is specific to RYTHMIQ (Boston Scientific), and DDI(R) only comes into play during mode switching for atrial arrhythmia. The aim of MVP is to reduce unnecessary right ventricular pacing, which is detrimental to LV function and associated with AF.
prog-ma-001.aRetenir: MVP operates in AAI(R) with ventricular monitoring and only switches to DDD(R) in the event of AV block.

prog-ma-002.question: What criterion causes a Medtronic pacemaker in MVP mode to switch from AAI(R)+ to DDD(R) operation?
options: Three slow ventricular beats within an 11-cycle window
No conduction in 3 of the last 8 atrial cycles
No ventricular sensed event in 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals
Two consecutive non-conducted P waves (complete AV block criterion)
commentaires: Incorrect: 3 slow beats out of 11 is the switching criterion of RYTHMIQ (Boston Scientific).
Incorrect: resumption of pacing after 3 out of 8 cycles without conduction corresponds to the standard setting of Vp Suppression (Biotronik).
Correct: MVP switches to DDD(R) when 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals contain no ventricular sensed event (2:1 AV block or worse than 4:3).
Incorrect: "2 consecutive blocked P waves" is the complete AV block criterion of SafeR (MicroPort), not that of MVP.
prog-ma-002.explication: MVP deliberately tolerates a single non-conducted P wave: this is what distinguishes it from AV hysteresis algorithms. The switch to DDD(R) occurs when the device finds no ventricular sensed event in 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals, corresponding to 2:1 AV block or an A:V ratio lower than 4:3. Each manufacturer has its own criteria, a frequent source of confusion in the device clinic: 2 consecutive blocked P waves for SafeR (MicroPort), 3 slow beats out of 11 for RYTHMIQ (Boston Scientific), cycles without conduction over an 8-cycle window for Vp Suppression (Biotronik). A programmable limit on the conducted A-V interval exists only as an option in the recent version ("MVP 2.0", devices marketed from 2017 onwards): the switch then also occurs if 2 of 4 A-V intervals exceed this limit.
prog-ma-002.aRetenir: MVP: switches to DDD(R) if there is no ventricular sensed event in 2 of the last 4 A-A intervals.

prog-ma-003.question: Medtronic pacemaker in MVP: a Holter recording shows a single P wave followed by neither a QRS nor a ventricular spike; the next P wave is then followed by ventricular pacing with a very short AV delay (about 80 ms). This is normal device behaviour.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: MVP tolerates a single non-conducted P wave, then delivers ventricular backup pacing with an 80 ms AV delay after the next atrial event: this is its normal behaviour.
Incorrect: concluding that there is undersensing, loss of capture or device failure is the classic pitfall; only repetition (2 cycles out of 4) causes a switch to DDD(R).
prog-ma-003.explication: This is normal MVP behaviour. After a non-conducted P wave, the device does not pace the ventricle in the same cycle, but delivers a backup ventricular pacing pulse with an AV delay of 80 ms after the next atrial event. This 80 ms delay was chosen as the shortest AV delay known to be asymptomatic. The classic pitfall is to conclude that there is undersensing, loss of capture or device malfunction. If, however, these cycles recur (2 out of 4), the device switches to DDD(R).
prog-ma-003.aRetenir: In MVP, a single blocked P wave followed by ventricular backup pacing with an 80 ms AV delay is normal and must not be mistaken for a malfunction.

prog-ma-004.question: After an MVP switch to DDD(R) for AV block, how does the Medtronic device test for the return of AV conduction?
options: Periodic AV delay extension, for up to 8 cycles, to look for a QRS
Return to AAI after 25 hysteresis cycles with fewer than 2 of 10 V paced
Return to AAI after 12 intrinsic QRS or every 100 paced cycles
Withholding one V pulse at 1 min, then at doubling intervals up to 16 h
commentaires: Incorrect: periodic AV delay extension for up to 8 cycles is how AV Search+ (Boston Scientific) works.
Incorrect: this is the condition for RYTHMIQ to return to AAI(R), which relies on AV Search+ (Boston Scientific).
Incorrect: 12 intrinsic ventricular events or a test every 100 paced cycles are the SafeR (MicroPort) criteria for returning to AAI.
Correct: MVP occasionally withholds a ventricular pacing pulse to test conduction, at 1 min and then at doubling intervals, up to 16 h.
prog-ma-004.explication: MVP performs periodic conduction checks by occasionally withholding a ventricular pacing pulse. The first check takes place 1 minute after the switch, then the interval doubles after each failure (2, 4, 8 minutes…) up to a maximum of 16 hours. If conduction has returned, the device reverts to AAI(R)+. Other manufacturers test conduction differently: SafeR (MicroPort) returns to AAI after 12 intrinsic QRS complexes or every 100 paced cycles, AV Search+ (Boston Scientific) periodically extends the AV delay, and RYTHMIQ relies on AV Search+ to return to AAI(R). In a patient with permanent complete AV block, MVP therefore remains in DDD(R) almost all the time, with only very infrequent conduction checks.
prog-ma-004.aRetenir: MVP conduction checks: at 1 min, then at doubling intervals, up to 16 h.

prog-ma-005.question: In the SAVE PACe trial (sinus node disease, preserved AV conduction), what was the effect of pacing designed to minimise ventricular pacing compared with conventional DDD?
options: A significant reduction in all-cause mortality and HF hospitalisations
Less persistent AF (relative reduction of about 40%), unchanged mortality
Fewer HF hospitalisations, with no significant effect on persistent AF
Much less RV pacing, but no significant effect on persistent AF
commentaires: Incorrect: mortality did not differ (4.9% vs 5.4%), and HF hospitalisations were not the key finding of the trial.
Correct: persistent AF 7.9% vs 12.7% (HR 0.60), with no difference in mortality.
Incorrect: it was the other way round: the benefit concerned persistent AF.
Incorrect: RV pacing did fall sharply (99% to 9.1%), but with a significant benefit on persistent AF; a neutral primary endpoint was the result of ANSWER (SafeR).
prog-ma-005.explication: SAVE PACe (1065 patients) compared dual-chamber pacing designed to minimise ventricular pacing with conventional DDD. The median percentage of ventricular pacing fell from 99% to 9.1%. Persistent AF occurred in 7.9% vs 12.7% of patients (HR 0.60: relative reduction of 40%, absolute reduction of 4.8%). Mortality did not differ (4.9% vs 5.4%). The benefit therefore concerns AF, not survival. Not to be confused with ANSWER (SafeR), in which the marked reduction in RV pacing did not translate into a significant effect on the composite primary endpoint.
prog-ma-005.aRetenir: SAVE PACe: reducing unnecessary RV pacing reduces persistent AF by 40%, with no effect on mortality.

prog-ma-006.question: What are the recognised limitations of, or precautions with, MVP mode? (select all that apply)
options: A very long PR interval tolerated over time can cause a "pseudo-pacemaker syndrome" picture
After a non-conducted P wave, a backup V pulse is delivered in the same cycle, 80 ms after that P wave
A blocked P wave creates a short-long-short sequence, which is proarrhythmic in some ICD patients
In permanent complete AV block, MVP keeps the device in AAI(R) most of the time
commentaires: Correct: MVP accepts even a very long PR interval; atrial contraction against a closed AV valve can cause symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome.
Incorrect: the ventricular backup pulse with an 80 ms AV delay is delivered after the next atrial event, not in the cycle of the blocked P wave: this is what creates the pause.
Correct: the pause caused by the blocked P wave can create a short-long-short sequence and promote pause-dependent VT.
Incorrect: in permanent complete AV block, the device remains in DDD(R) and performs only infrequent conduction checks.
prog-ma-006.explication: MVP favours intrinsic conduction, even with a very long PR interval: some patients then report symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome (atrial contraction against a closed AV valve). After a blocked P wave, the ventricular backup pulse is delivered only after the next atrial event, with an 80 ms AV delay: the blocked P wave therefore creates a pause, and a short-long-short sequence may trigger pause-dependent VT. This is why the "MVP 2.0" upgrade added, as an option, a programmable A-R interval limit (switch to DDD(R) when the A-R interval, tracked over several cycles, persistently exceeds it) as well as refinements that reduce long V-V intervals. In permanent complete AV block, the device remains in DDD(R) and performs only infrequent conduction checks.
prog-ma-006.aRetenir: MVP: beware of very long PR intervals and pauses (the V backup comes in the next cycle); in complete AV block, the device stays in DDD(R).

prog-ma-007.question: Medtronic automatic atrial threshold measurement (Atrial Capture Management) can use two methods to confirm capture. What are they, and on what principle is each based?
prog-ma-007.reponseAttendue: 1) Atrial Chamber Reset (ACR) method: the atrium is paced slightly faster than the sinus rate, and capture is confirmed by the absence of a sensed intrinsic P wave (the sinus cycle is "reset"). 2) AV Conduction (AVC) method: atrial capture is confirmed by the presence of a conducted ventricular response at the expected interval after the atrial pacing pulse. The choice depends on the underlying rhythm (stable sinus rhythm for ACR, reliable AV conduction for AVC).
prog-ma-007.explication: Unlike in the ventricle, the evoked P wave is too small to be detected reliably as an evoked response; Medtronic therefore uses indirect methods. The ACR method paces the atrium at a rate above the sinus rate: if the pulse captures, the atrium is depolarised and no intrinsic P wave appears. If the pulse fails to capture, a sinus P wave is sensed. The AVC method relies on AV conduction: a capturing atrial pulse is followed by a conducted QRS at a consistent interval. These tests are performed periodically, not on every cycle, and the amplitude is adjusted with a safety margin. Pitfall: the AVC method cannot be used in AV block.
prog-ma-007.aRetenir: Medtronic ACM confirms atrial capture by resetting the sinus rhythm (ACR) or by AV conduction (AVC), during periodic tests.

prog-ma-008.question: What is the principle of the Rate Drop Response algorithm in Medtronic pacemakers?
options: Lowering the lower rate during sleep hours programmed on the device clock
Regularising the ventricular response in conducted AF by increasing the pacing rate
Responding to an abrupt rate drop with transient high-rate pacing
Detecting the rise in contractility that precedes syncope and pacing faster before the drop
commentaires: Incorrect: the programmed night-time lowering of the lower rate is the Sleep function.
Incorrect: regularisation of conducted AF is the role of Conducted AF Response.
Correct: Rate Drop Response detects an abrupt drop (or a persistently low rate) and delivers high-rate intervention pacing.
Incorrect: anticipating syncope from contractility (intracardiac impedance) is the principle of Biotronik Closed Loop Stimulation.
prog-ma-008.explication: Rate Drop Response was designed for cardioinhibitory reflex (vasovagal) syncope. It detects an abrupt rate drop ("Drop Detection") or a persistently low rate ("Low Rate Detection"). It responds with high-rate intervention pacing for a programmed duration. Night-time rate lowering is the role of the Sleep function, and regularisation in AF is the role of Conducted AF Response. Anticipating syncope by measuring contractility is the principle of Biotronik Closed Loop Stimulation (SPAIN trial), not of Rate Drop Response. The latter was evaluated in VPS and VPS II. According to the 2018 ESC guidelines, pacing should be considered only in selected forms of documented cardioinhibitory reflex syncope.
prog-ma-008.aRetenir: Rate Drop Response responds to an abrupt rate drop with high-rate intervention pacing (cardioinhibitory syncope).

prog-ma-009.question: In the randomised double-blind VPS II trial (pacemaker implanted in all patients, DDD with rate drop response vs ODO), pacing significantly reduced recurrence of vasovagal syncope.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: it was VPS I, an open-label trial, that had shown a large benefit; under double-blind conditions, the reduction was not significant.
Correct: VPS II showed only a non-significant 30% relative reduction (one-sided p = 0.14), suggesting a placebo effect of implantation.
prog-ma-009.explication: This is false. VPS I, an open-label trial, had shown a large benefit. However, VPS II, which was double-blind (all patients implanted, device active or not), showed only a non-significant 30% relative reduction in time to syncope recurrence (one-sided p = 0.14). This discrepancy suggests a substantial placebo effect of implantation in open-label trials. The authors concluded that pacing should not be offered as first-line therapy for recurrent vasovagal syncope. The 2018 ESC guidelines reserve it for selected patients: aged over 40, with severe syncope and documented asystole.
prog-ma-009.aRetenir: VPS II (double-blind): no significant reduction in vasovagal syncope with rate drop response pacing.

prog-ma-010.question: The Sleep function in Medtronic pacemakers lowers the lower rate when the accelerometer detects a prolonged period of rest.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the Sleep function does not depend on measured activity; lowering the rate when the sensor detects rest corresponds to Abbott Rest Rate.
Correct: the Sleep function applies a lower rate between a programmed bedtime and wake time, based on the device clock.
prog-ma-010.explication: This is false. The Sleep function applies a lower base rate (Sleep Rate) between a programmed bedtime and wake time, to reflect the physiological night-time fall in heart rate. It relies on the device clock, not on the patient's actual activity. Rate lowering triggered by the activity sensor is the logic of Abbott Rest Rate. Practical consequence: the Sleep function times need to be adjusted in night-shift workers or after a change of time zone. It avoids unnecessary night-time pacing, which may be poorly tolerated and drains the battery.
prog-ma-010.aRetenir: The Medtronic Sleep function lowers the lower rate according to programmed times, not according to detected activity.

prog-ma-011.question: Explain the principle of the Conducted AF Response algorithm in Medtronic devices (particularly in CRT) and its purpose.
prog-ma-011.reponseAttendue: In conducted AF, the algorithm increases the ventricular pacing rate when conducted intrinsic ventricular events are sensed, then gradually decreases it. The ventricular response is thus regularised, with more paced cycles: in CRT, this increases the percentage of biventricular pacing during AF.
prog-ma-011.explication: In AF, irregular AV conduction competes with pacing and reduces the percentage of biventricular pacing, whereas CRT requires near-continuous pacing. Conducted AF Response increases the pacing rate on each conducted ventricular sensed event, then brings it back down: the mean rate rises slightly and more cycles are paced. In the CRTee trial, this algorithm was the comparator for a more recent algorithm (EffectivCRT during AF), based on actual LV capture effectiveness. The latter further increased the percentage of effective CRT, at the cost of a +2.5 bpm increase in mean rate. Pitfall: no algorithm is a substitute for rate control or AV junction ablation when biventricular pacing remains insufficient.
prog-ma-011.aRetenir: Conducted AF Response regularises conducted AF by transiently increasing the pacing rate, which increases the pacing percentage (biventricular in CRT).

prog-ma-012.question: Atrial Preference Pacing (APP, Medtronic) paces the atrium slightly above the sinus rate to prevent AF. What does the meta-analysis of randomised trials of this type of algorithm show?
options: Fewer PACs, but no reduction in AF burden
Less permanent AF at 2 years, with no effect on PACs
Lower cardiovascular mortality in sinus node dysfunction
Significantly lower AF burden and less progression to permanent AF
commentaires: Correct: in the Munawar meta-analysis, these algorithms reduced PAC burden without reducing AF burden or the number of AF episodes.
Incorrect: it is the other way round; the reduction in permanent AF observed in MINERVA is attributed to reactive atrial ATP, not to preventive pacing.
Incorrect: no effect on mortality has been shown with preventive atrial pacing.
Incorrect: the meta-analysis shows neither a reduction in AF burden nor a slowing of progression to permanent AF.
prog-ma-012.explication: Atrial Preference Pacing maintains atrial pacing slightly above the sinus rate, by increasing the rate after an intrinsic atrial sensed event and then gradually decreasing it. In the Munawar meta-analysis (21 randomised trials), APP algorithms reduced PAC burden but not AF burden or the number of AF episodes. Prevention algorithms alone did not prevent AF progression; in MINERVA, the slowing of progression to permanent AF is instead attributed to reactive atrial ATP. No effect on mortality or heart failure has been shown. In practice, these algorithms are not routinely activated to prevent AF.
prog-ma-012.aRetenir: Preventive atrial pacing reduces PACs but not AF burden.

prog-ma-013.question: What is the principle of the Medtronic Rate Stabilization function (atrial or ventricular), and which arrhythmia is it intended to prevent?
prog-ma-013.reponseAttendue: After a premature beat (PAC or PVC), the algorithm shortens the next escape interval to avoid the compensatory pause, thereby abolishing the short-long-short sequence. It targets pause-triggered arrhythmias: AF for the atrial version, pause-dependent VT/VF for the ventricular version (ICD).
prog-ma-013.explication: Many arrhythmias start after a short-long-short sequence: a premature beat (short), followed by a compensatory pause (long), then a premature beat that triggers the arrhythmia. Rate Stabilization adjusts the escape interval following the premature beat to avoid this pause. In a prospective crossover study of 309 ICD patients, ventricular rate stabilisation did not significantly reduce VT/VF recurrence. During the phase without stabilisation, only 8% of the episodes analysed (36 of 427) actually started after a pause. This algorithm is therefore reserved for patients whose stored EGMs show pause-dependent arrhythmias. Pitfall: it increases pacing, and therefore RV pacing in the ventricular version.
prog-ma-013.aRetenir: Rate Stabilization abolishes the post-ectopic pause; its value is limited to arrhythmias proven to be pause-dependent.

prog-ma-014.question: What distinguishes Reactive ATP in Medtronic pacemakers from conventional atrial ATP?
options: It avoids pacing the atrium in its vulnerable period after a PAC
It re-attempts atrial ATP when the rhythm organises or after a set delay
It delivers low-energy atrial cardioversion if ATP fails
It paces the atrium just above the sinus rate to prevent AF
commentaires: Incorrect: avoiding the atrial vulnerable period after a PAC is the role of PAC Response (Abbott).
Correct: Reactive ATP re-attempts ATP sequences during an episode when the cycle length increases or becomes more regular, or after a delay.
Incorrect: a pacemaker does not deliver shocks; internal atrial cardioversion was available only in older atrial defibrillators.
Incorrect: atrial pacing just above the sinus rate is the preventive principle of Atrial Preference Pacing, not a treatment.
prog-ma-014.explication: Conventional atrial ATP is delivered at the onset of an atrial tachycardia episode and then abandoned if unsuccessful. Reactive ATP re-attempts therapy during the episode when the rhythm evolves towards a more organised form (longer, more regular cycle) or after a programmed delay. In MINERVA, high Reactive ATP efficacy was associated with less persistent or permanent AF. A pacemaker does not deliver shocks. Atrial Preference Pacing (prevention by overdrive) and Abbott PAC Response (avoiding the vulnerable period after a PAC) are separate preventive functions. Reactive ATP is most effective on organised atrial tachycardias and atrial flutter, much less so on AF.
prog-ma-014.aRetenir: Reactive ATP re-attempts atrial ATP when the arrhythmia organises, to target atrial tachycardias and flutter.

prog-ma-015.question: In the MINERVA trial (Medtronic pacemakers, history of atrial tachyarrhythmias), what result was observed?
options: Conventional DDDR outperformed the other two arms on permanent AF
MVP alone significantly reduced the composite endpoint vs DDDR
No arm altered progression to permanent AF or the composite
DDDRP + MVP reduced the composite, mainly via permanent AF
commentaires: Incorrect: conventional DDDR was the control arm and did not perform better on any endpoint.
Incorrect: the MVP-alone arm was not significantly different from DDDR (HR 0.89).
Incorrect: the DDDRP + MVP arm reduced permanent AF (HR 0.39) and the composite endpoint.
Correct: 19.8% vs 26.5% (HR 0.74), a benefit driven mainly by the reduction in permanent AF.
prog-ma-015.explication: MINERVA randomised 1166 patients to conventional DDDR, MVP alone or DDDRP + MVP (preventive algorithms and atrial ATP, including Reactive ATP). The 2-year composite endpoint was reduced in the DDDRP + MVP arm (19.8% vs 26.5%; HR 0.74). The MVP-alone arm was not significantly different from DDDR (HR 0.89). The benefit came mainly from a reduction in permanent AF (HR 0.39) and in AF lasting more than 7 days. This result is often attributed to reactive atrial ATP rather than to preventive pacing, which is of little efficacy in meta-analysis.
prog-ma-015.aRetenir: MINERVA: DDDRP + MVP (with Reactive ATP) delays progression to permanent AF; MVP alone is not enough.
